The exquisite gentlemen of the most refined breeding wore dangling ornaments that tinkled with their languid movements. Their golden chains chimed like costly little bells, and the mingled ringing and rustling of silk, brocade, and delicate linen stirred the air sufficiently to waft Saint Antoine and his ravenous hunger far away.

Clothing was the infallible talisman employed to preserve the proper order of things. Everyone was costumed for a Fancy Ball destined never to end. From the Tuileries Palace, through Monseigneur and the entire Court, through the Chambers, the courts of law, and every rank of society except the scarecrows, this masquerade extended even to the Common Executioner. To maintain the spell, he must perform his duties “curled, powdered, in a gold-trimmed coat, pumps, and white silk stockings.” At the gallows and the wheel—the axe was seldom used—Monsieur Paris presided in this elegant attire. Such was his episcopal style of address among his provincial fellow Professors, Monsieur Orleans and the rest. And who at Monseigneur’s reception, in that year of our Lord seventeen hundred and eighty, could question that a system founded upon a powdered, curled, gold-braided hangman in pumps and white silk stockings would outlast the stars themselves?

Having relieved his four attendants of their burdens and consumed his chocolate, Monseigneur ordered the doors of the Holiest of Holies opened and emerged. What submission followed, what crouching, flattery, servitude, and utter self-abasement! So completely did body and spirit bow that nothing remained for Heaven, perhaps one reason among others why Monseigneur’s worshippers never troubled it.

With a promising word for this one and a smile for that, a whisper to one fortunate slave and a gesture to another, Monseigneur graciously traversed his apartments as far as the distant Circumference of Truth. There he turned and retraced his steps until, in due time, the chocolate spirits enclosed him once more in his sanctuary, and he disappeared.

The performance finished, the stirring air became a small tempest, and those precious bells jingled down the stairs. Soon only one of the company remained. With hat beneath his arm and snuff-box in hand, he moved slowly among the mirrors towards the exit.

“I consign you,” he said, pausing at the final doorway and facing the sanctuary, “to the Devil!”

Then he flicked the snuff from his fingers as though shaking dust from his feet, and descended the stairs quietly.

The only difficulty that seemed to concern him was choosing whom to kill. He understood that murder, like pagan religion, required a victim as well as a priest. Since he was no genius, he had no enemies. Besides, he felt this was no occasion to indulge personal resentment or dislike; his mission was too deeply serious and solemn. He therefore listed his friends and relatives on a sheet of writing paper. After careful thought, he chose Lady Clementina Beauchamp, a dear old woman living in Curzon Street, and his second cousin on his mother’s side. He had always loved Lady Clem, as everyone called her. Since he was wealthy himself, having inherited all Lord Rugby’s property when he came of age, her death could offer him no vulgar financial advantage. Indeed, the more he considered it, the more perfectly suitable she seemed. Feeling that any delay would be unfair to Sybil, he decided to begin making arrangements immediately.

First, of course, he had to pay the palm reader. He sat at a small Sheraton writing desk by the window and wrote a check for £105 to Mr. Septimus Podgers. After placing it in an envelope, he instructed his valet to deliver it to West Moon Street. Then he telephoned the stables for his hansom cab and dressed to go out. As he left the room, he looked back at Sybil Merton’s photograph and vowed that, whatever happened, he would never reveal what he was doing for her. He would keep the secret of his self-sacrifice forever hidden in his heart.

On his way to the Buckingham, he stopped at a florist and sent Sybil a beautiful basket of narcissus flowers, their lovely white petals surrounding bright pheasant’s-eye centers. At the club he went directly to the library, rang the bell, and asked the waiter for a lemon-and-soda and a book on poisons. He had decided that poison was the best way to handle this troublesome business. Any sort of physical violence disgusted him. He was also anxious to avoid killing Lady Clementina in a way that attracted public attention, since he hated the thought of becoming the center of interest at Lady Windermere’s or seeing his name in the columns of vulgar society newspapers.

If he asked why I desired it, or what right I imagined I possessed, I would tell him—though he valued such poor dreams so little—that I had loved Estella deeply and for many years. Though I had lost her and must lead a bereaved existence, everything touching her remained dearer and closer to me than anything else on earth. Mr. Jaggers received this appeal in perfect stillness and silence, apparently unmoved. I therefore turned to Wemmick. “Wemmick, I know your heart is kind. I have visited your agreeable home, met your elderly father, and witnessed the innocent, happy playfulness with which you relieve your working life. I beg you to speak on my behalf to Mr. Jaggers, and persuade him that, considering everything, he ought to treat me with greater openness!”

Never have I seen two men exchange stranger glances than Wemmick and Mr. Jaggers did after this address. For an instant I feared Wemmick would lose his employment immediately; that fear disappeared when Mr. Jaggers softened into something resembling a smile and Wemmick grew more confident.

“What is this?” asked Mr. Jaggers. “You possess an old father, and pleasant, playful habits?”

“Well,” Wemmick answered, “if I leave them outside this office, what harm is done?”

“Pip,” Mr. Jaggers said, putting a hand on my arm and smiling plainly now, “this fellow must be London’s most artful impostor.”

“Nothing of the kind,” returned Wemmick, becoming steadily bolder. “I fancy you’re another.”

They exchanged those odd glances again, each still appearing to suspect the other of deceiving him.

“You have a pleasant home?” Mr. Jaggers asked.

“As it doesn’t obstruct business,” said Wemmick, “let it stand. Looking at you now, sir, I shouldn’t be surprised if you were planning a pleasant home yourself one day, when this work has tired you out.”

Mr. Jaggers nodded two or three times, as though looking back, and actually sighed. “Pip,” he said, “we shall leave ‘poor dreams’ alone. Your experience is much fresher than mine, and you understand them better. But as for the other business, I will propose a case. Remember, I acknowledge nothing.”

He paused until I confirmed that I understood his express declaration that he acknowledged nothing.

“Suppose this case, Pip,” he continued. “Suppose a woman in the circumstances you have described concealed her child, and had to tell her legal adviser when he explained that the scope of his defence required him to know the facts concerning that child.
